questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a primary key commits a table to
questions.learningObjective: say what a primary key guarantees and what it does not
questions.stem: A team adds a primary key to the member_id column of a table that already holds 500 rows, and the statement is accepted. What does the acceptance of that statement tell you about the column?

options.text: The column already holds 500 distinct non-null values, so every row can be addressed on its own
The column holds 500 values that are all different from each other in spelling, though several may be blank
options.misconception: reads a uniqueness check as if it also proved every value is present

options.text: The column holds 500 values and none of them repeats, but blanks are still allowed because blanks are not a value
options.misconception: believes a key can tolerate missing values in the rows it governs

options.text: The column holds 500 values that sort into a single fixed order, which is a stronger promise than uniqueness
options.misconception: confuses the ordering a key provides with the uniqueness it provides

questions.explanation: A primary key is two promises at once: no two rows may carry the same value, and no row may leave it empty. The database checks both before it will accept the constraint, so a statement that succeeds is evidence that all 500 existing rows satisfied both. What it does not promise is anything about the meaning of the values, that they were entered correctly, or that they will keep their format, since a key of the wrong type can be perfectly unique and perfectly wrong. The other three options each keep one half of the promise and quietly drop the other, which is exactly the shape of the bug that appears later when a join cannot find the row it was promised.
questions.hint: Count the promises a key makes about a column, then ask which of them the accepted statement would have had to check.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a foreign key rules out
questions.learningObjective: name the mistake a foreign key makes impossible
questions.stem: An orders table declares customer_id as a foreign key onto the customer table's primary key. A nightly load then tries to insert an order for customer_id 8814, which appears nowhere in the customer table. What happens to that row?

options.text: The row is accepted and stores 8814, because a number of the right shape is a valid reference by itself
options.misconception: believes a reference only has to look like a key to count as one

options.text: The row is accepted but the reference is stored as text, so a later join can decide for itself what to do with it
options.misconception: believes the constraint changes the stored type instead of rejecting the write

options.text: The row is rejected, and any order for a customer who was never loaded cannot enter the table at all
The row is accepted only if the customer is created in the same statement, so ordering inside one load is what matters
options.misconception: thinks the check only applies to changes made inside a single statement

questions.explanation: A foreign key turns a relationship between two tables into something the database itself will not let you get wrong, which means an insert naming a parent row that does not exist fails outright rather than leaving a reference that resolves to nothing. That is the whole value of declaring it: the orphan row never enters, so no later report has to wonder whether a missing parent is a real gap or a load that ran early. The cost of the guarantee is that load order starts to matter, since a customer arriving after its orders cannot be written first, and teams often respond by disabling the constraint, which is the moment the guarantee quietly stops existing.
questions.hint: Ask what the database can do at insert time that it could not do if the relationship were only a naming convention.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What an inner join drops
questions.learningObjective: say which side of an inner join can lose rows
questions.stem: A report joins orders to customers with an inner join on customer_id. The orders table holds six rows and three of them name customers the customer table does not contain. What does the join return?

options.text: Three rows, being only the orders whose customer_id was found in the customer table
options.misconception: believes an inner join keeps the left table and fills the gaps instead of dropping them

options.text: Six rows, with the three unmatched orders carrying blanks in the customer columns
Nine rows, because each of the six orders is paired with every one of the three matching customers
options.misconception: treats a join as a cross product rather than a lookup on a matching value

options.text: Six rows, but the three unmatched orders are moved to the end of the result by the join itself
options.misconception: assumes the join sorts unmatched rows somewhere rather than discarding them

questions.explanation: An inner join keeps a row only when both sides of the condition can be satisfied, so the three orders naming customers that do not exist have nothing to pair with and disappear without a trace. The result is three rows, and the danger is not the loss itself but that the loss is invisible in the output: the report simply says three orders exist, and the count of six never appears anywhere to be contradicted. This is why an inner join is a filter as much as a lookup, and why anyone reporting a figure from one should say which side was allowed to vanish. The trap is assuming the left table is protected, which is true of a left join and false here.
questions.hint: Ask what an unmatched row on either side has to pair with in order to survive an inner join.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a left join introduces
questions.learningObjective: say what a left join guarantees and what it puts in the result
questions.stem: A report changes to a left join from orders to customers, and now every one of the six orders appears. One order names a customer who is not in the customer table. What does that order look like in the result?

options.text: It appears with a zero in every customer column, which is why sums over those columns stay correct
options.misconception: expects a missing parent to be filled with a number that behaves like a real value

options.text: It appears with a blank in every column taken from the customer table, and every later calculation must decide what that means
It does not appear, because a row with nothing to pair with cannot be given a customer name at all
options.misconception: applies inner-join reasoning to a join that was explicitly written to keep the left side

options.text: It appears once for every row in the customer table, each copy carrying that customer's name in turn
options.misconception: reads a left join as a cross join with the left table on top

questions.explanation: The point of a left join is that the left row survives whether or not anything matches, and the cost of that guarantee is that the columns coming from the other side can hold no value at all. A blank is not a zero and not an empty string: it is the absence of an answer, and arithmetic that meets one either refuses to run or quietly treats the row as excluded, which changes totals in ways nobody notices until a report is wrong. The habit worth building is to ask, immediately after writing a left join, which columns can now be blank and which downstream figures assumed they never would be, because the join changed the meaning of the data rather than only its shape.
questions.hint: Separate the guarantee the join makes about row counts from the guarantee it makes about values.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Row multiplication on a non-unique column
questions.learningObjective: predict the row count a join produces from both sides' multiplicities
questions.stem: A sales table has five orders, three of them in region West. A reps table lists four reps and two of them are both assigned to West. Joining sales to reps on region alone, with nothing else to separate the reps, produces how many rows?

options.text: Five rows, because each order should still be matched to the one rep that owns it
options.misconception: assumes a join matches each left row to exactly one right row no matter how many candidates exist

options.text: Eight rows, because each of the three West orders is paired once with each of the two West reps
Twenty rows, because every order is being paired with every rep and then filtered afterwards by eye
options.misconception: counts the full cross product and forgets that a join condition still applies

options.text: Twelve rows, because the four reps multiply the five orders once and the two extra West reps add three more on top
options.misconception: adds the multiplication and the duplicate count instead of choosing one of them

questions.explanation: A join emits one row for every pair of rows that satisfies the condition, so the row count is a product taken group by group: three West orders each find two matching reps and so contribute six rows, the East order contributes one, and the North order contributes one, giving eight rows from five orders. Nothing about the join is broken; it is doing exactly what it was asked, and the mistake was asking a question the condition cannot answer, because region alone does not say which rep owns an order. Any figure taken from this result is now wrong in a way that is hard to see: the total is larger, no value looks impossible, and the only symptom is that revenue per order has quietly fallen.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of matching right-hand rows by the number of left rows for each value of the join column, then add.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Which rows an aggregate after a join sees
questions.learningObjective: trace how a duplicating join changes what a sum is summing
questions.stem: A query joins sales to reps on region and then reports SUM of the order amount for every region. The West orders total 660 and the other two regions total 130. What does the West row of that report show?

options.text: 1320, because the two West reps have each been credited with the whole West total
660, because the sum is taken over order amounts and the reps table contributes no amounts of its own
options.misconception: believes a sum is immune to a join that duplicates the rows it reads

options.text: 330, because splitting 660 between two reps is what a grouped report is for
options.misconception: divides a figure by the number of matching rows as if grouping were an allocation

options.text: 790, because the report adds all three regions together and shows the same total on every region row
options.misconception: reads one group's row as though it held the whole table's total

questions.explanation: The sum has no idea which table an amount came from, so it adds every amount row the join handed it, and the join handed it each West amount twice because two reps share the region. The West row therefore reports 1320 while the ledger says 660, and nothing in the output is malformed: the number is an honest sum over a result set that was already wrong. This is the most expensive join mistake in practice because it survives every format check and every sanity check a reader applies, and it is fixed not by adjusting the sum but by making the join return each order once, usually by aggregating the reps table to one row per region before joining or by joining on something that actually identifies a rep.
questions.hint: Ask how many copies of each West amount the join placed in the result set, and let the sum do the rest.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Filtering before or after an aggregate
questions.learningObjective: predict what changes when a filter moves across an aggregate
questions.stem: A report must count only orders over 100. Written one way it filters the rows and then adds up what survives; written another it adds up everything and then discards the groups that fall short. Where does the two versions part company?

options.text: Nowhere, because a row either passes the threshold or does not regardless of when the test is applied
options.misconception: believes the position of a filter relative to an aggregate changes nothing

options.text: On rows that never passed the threshold but inflate a group total, which the filtered version can no longer recover
Only on groups whose filtered total falls below the threshold, since unfiltered totals are always larger
options.misconception: sees the difference only where the filtered version rejects the whole group

options.text: On the count of qualifying rows, since the filtered version tallies rows and the other tallies groups
options.misconception: believes the two versions are counting different units rather than filtering at different moments

questions.explanation: Filtering rows first and filtering groups afterwards are different questions, and the second one cannot see the small rows at all, so anything they contributed is gone for good rather than merely excluded. If a group of six orders totalling 835 is cut to three orders totalling 620, a filter applied afterwards sees only 620 and has no way to know that 215 of the total was made of rows it would have discarded, which is exactly why a group can fail a threshold in one version and pass it in the other. The practical rule is to decide whether the condition is about rows or about groups, and to write it in the clause that matches, because the two positions are not interchangeable.
questions.hint: Ask which version still has the discarded rows available to it when the threshold is applied.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Subquery in a filter versus a join
questions.learningObjective: choose between a subquery and a join for the same comparison
questions.stem: A report must list the orders whose amount exceeds the average order amount. Written with a subquery in the filter it compares each row to a single figure; written as a join to that figure it produces the same comparison. What distinguishes the two forms in practice?

options.text: Nothing distinguishes them, since both compute one average and compare every row against the same number
options.misconception: believes a subquery and a join always return an identically shaped result

options.text: The subquery keeps the result at one row per order, while a join to a single figure can multiply rows if the figure is not reduced first
The subquery is slower in every case, because a filter written as a join is always cheaper to evaluate
options.misconception: believes a syntactic difference guarantees a performance difference in one direction

options.text: The join cannot express the comparison at all, since a join matches values rather than testing them against a bound
options.misconception: thinks a comparison against a constant cannot be written as a join condition

questions.explanation: Both forms express the same test, and the difference shows up in what the result set is allowed to contain. A subquery in the filter never adds a row, so the output is one row per order whatever the subquery computed, which makes the shape of the answer predictable. A join against a derived figure is safe only while that derived side is guaranteed to be one row per match, and the moment it is not, the same duplication that inflates a sum starts inflating a list, and a report that promised one line per order delivers two or three. Knowing which form keeps the row count honest is worth more than knowing which one the planner prefers, because the planner can be asked and the row count cannot be assumed.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two forms can add rows to the result, and under what condition.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: How often a correlated subquery runs
questions.learningObjective: predict the number of evaluations a correlated subquery performs
questions.stem: A report selects five rows from a parent table and, for each one, runs a subquery that refers back to the outer row's own department. How many times does the inner query actually execute?

options.text: Once, because the database can rewrite the correlated reference into a single grouped lookup
options.misconception: assumes every correlated subquery is rewritten into a plan computed once

options.text: Five times, once for each outer row, because the value it depends on is not known until that row is read
Ten times, once for each outer row and once more to confirm that no further matches exist
options.misconception: invents a confirmation pass that no part of the query describes

options.text: Once per row in the inner table as well, so the count depends on the size of both tables together
options.misconception: believes the outer row count is multiplied by the inner row count

questions.explanation: A correlated subquery refers to the row currently being processed on the outside, so its text cannot be turned into a single plan step decided in advance; it runs again for every outer row, which here means five executions. Some engines will rewrite a particular correlated form into a join or a grouped lookup and pay for it once, and when that happens the behaviour is an optimisation rather than a promise, so the number that should appear in a written explanation is the logical one. The practical consequence is a cost that scales with the outer table, which is why a correlated filter over a large table is one of the most reliable ways to write a query that used to be fine and is not any more.
questions.hint: Ask when the value the inner query depends on becomes known.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Window function against group-by
questions.learningObjective: say what a window function keeps that a group-by discards
questions.stem: A report needs each order's amount together with the average amount of its own region, while still listing every order. Which construct was written for that requirement?

options.text: A group-by with the region in the select list, which returns the average once per region and lists the orders
options.misconception: believes a grouped result can still contain one row per original order

options.text: A window function partitioned by region, which computes the regional average while leaving every order in the output
A correlated subquery in the select list, which is the only construct that can produce a per-row figure
options.misconception: believes a per-row figure requires a subquery and cannot be expressed any other way

options.text: A left join to a table of regional averages, which returns the average beside each order without any grouping
options.misconception: misses that a joined average is still a value that must be produced by grouping somewhere

questions.explanation: The requirement is contradictory to a group-by and ordinary to a window function: a group-by collapses several rows into one, so the moment you ask for the regional average alongside every individual order you have asked for a figure that is attached to a group while the rows remain separate. A window function does precisely that, computing something across a set of rows while leaving those rows themselves in the result, and the partition is what says which set. The convenience is that the same query can carry several such figures at once, so a rank, a running total and a group average can all be reported without three passes and without a join that might duplicate rows.
questions.hint: Ask which construct can compute a group-level value without removing the rows that formed the group.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a window frame can see
questions.learningObjective: read a window frame boundary correctly
questions.stem: A running total is written with a frame running from the start of the partition up to the current row, and the rows are ordered by day. On the third of four days, which rows does the frame contain?

options.text: The first and second rows only, because the upper bound of a frame stops one row short of the current row
options.misconception: reads the stated upper bound as exclusive and drops the current row from its own total

options.text: The first, second and third rows, because the current row is the upper bound of its own frame
All four rows, because a running total in a partition always sees the whole partition
options.misconception: believes any partition-level function ignores the frame it was given

options.text: The third row only, because the frame covers the current row and nothing that came before it
options.misconception: assumes the lower bound of a running frame is the current row rather than the partition start

questions.explanation: A frame says which rows a windowed function may look at, and the bounds written in it are the bounds that apply, not a hint. Between the start of the partition and the current row, stated in that order, the current row is included: the boundary is the current row, so on the third day the total covers days one, two and three, and only the final row of the partition is a whole-partition total. Reading an upper bound as exclusive is the common slip, and it produces a series that is one row short at every step, which is easy to mistake for a data problem because the shape of the line still looks like a running total. The habit that prevents it is to write the bounds out loud in words before trusting the numbers.
questions.hint: Write the frame in words first, then ask whether the current row falls inside it.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Rank, dense rank and row number
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the three ranking functions by what they do with ties
questions.stem: Four rows score 90, 85, 85 and 70 in that order. Which of the three ranking functions returns 3 for the first of the two rows that both scored 85?

options.text: DENSE_RANK, because it numbers distinct score values without leaving gaps after a tie
RANK, because it counts the rows ahead of a tied score rather than the distinct values ahead of it
options.misconception: believes rank numbers distinct values instead of counting rows above the tie

options.text: ROW_NUMBER, because it numbers positions and so breaks a tie by position in the sort order
options.misconception: expects row_number to be a function of the score rather than of the order

options.text: None of them, because a tie in a score cannot be numbered at all without an arbitrary rule to break it
options.misconception: believes a tie leaves a ranking function with nothing to return

questions.explanation: The three functions differ only in what they do about equality, and picking between them is mostly a question of whether gaps in the numbering matter to the reader. RANK counts rows above, so a tie at 85 following 90 yields 2 for both tied rows and then 4 for the next, because the two rows ahead of 70 occupy two places. DENSE_RANK counts distinct values, giving 2, 2 and then 3, which is what a leaderboard wants. ROW_NUMBER ignores the tie entirely and hands out consecutive positions, 1, 2, 3, 4, which is what a report wanting exactly one row per group needs. Choosing RANK where DENSE_RANK was meant produces a list whose numbers appear to skip for no visible reason.
questions.hint: Ask whether the function counts rows above the value or distinct values above it.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The base case a recursive query needs
questions.learningObjective: say what a recursive query must be given before it can recurse
questions.stem: A recursive query walks a management hierarchy from the top of the tree downwards, adding one level of reports at each pass. What must the query be given before the recursion can begin?

options.text: The set of rows that start the walk, so there is something to add to on the first pass
A maximum depth, so the query knows how many times it is allowed to add another level of reports
options.misconception: believes a recursive query needs a depth limit before it can start

options.text: An empty result, so the recursion can be tested against a case where nothing has been found yet
options.misconception: thinks a recursive query must be handed an empty set to begin

options.text: A list of every manager in the table, so the query knows the whole shape of the tree in advance
options.misconception: assumes the tree must be fully described before any level of it can be read

questions.explanation: A recursive query is a loop with two halves, and the first half is not optional: the anchor, the rows the walk starts from, which is the only place a value can enter the result. Without it the loop has nothing to add to and returns nothing at all, which is the usual reason a recursive query over a hierarchy returns an empty result rather than an error. The second half is the recursive step, which reads what the previous pass produced and adds a further level, and the two together are repeated until a pass adds no rows, at which point the walk is finished. What the query does not need is a description of the tree, a depth limit, or a seed row: it needs an entry point and a stopping condition.
questions.hint: Ask where the first value in the result comes from, since a loop cannot begin without one.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a named subquery buys the reader
questions.learningObjective: say what a named subquery changes for the person reading the query
questions.stem: A six-way join is rewritten so that each step is a named intermediate result that the next step selects from. The computed answers are identical. What has the rewrite bought?

options.text: A shorter runtime, because a named intermediate result lets the database skip work it would otherwise repeat
options.misconception: believes the only benefit of naming a step is that the database can optimise it away

options.text: A place to name and check each step, so a wrong figure can be located in a named step rather than in a wall of joins
A guarantee that the result cannot contain duplicate rows, because each step returns a distinct result
options.misconception: assumes naming a step enforces uniqueness on what it returns

options.text: A guarantee that the joins are correct, because the database validates the named steps against each other
options.misconception: believes naming a step makes the logic checkable automatically

questions.explanation: A named intermediate result is a label attached to a set of rows, and its value is almost entirely social: it lets the writer say what each step is meant to contain, check the count and the shape of that step on its own, and point at the one place where a figure went wrong. Six joins written inline are not wrong because they are long, they are hard to debug because every output column is a function of all six tables at once, and a miscount cannot be localised. The rewrite changes no answers and guarantees nothing about speed or correctness, which is exactly why it is worth doing: the parts of a query you can inspect are the parts you can repair.
questions.hint: Ask what changes for the person trying to find the mistake, since the computed answers are the same.

questions.topic: Rows surviving a key constraint
questions.learningObjective: compute the row count left after a key rejects duplicates
questions.stem: A member table holds 500 rows and its member_id is the primary key. A batch of 7 rows arrives, and three of them carry a member_id that is already in the table. How many rows does the table hold once the batch has been written?
questions.explanation: The key refuses the three duplicates outright, so the table keeps its 500 rows and gains only the 4 rows in the batch that carry a key it has not seen, giving 504. The two routes agree: loading the batch into a set of existing keys and adding only unseen ones leaves 504 distinct keys, while 500 plus the 4 accepted rows also gives 504. The count of 7 is a red herring that a great many students subtract from the total, producing 493, and the reason that number is wrong is that the rejected rows never entered the table, so there is nothing to subtract from it.

questions.stem: A ticket table holds six rows whose agent_id values are 21, 22, 21, 23, 24 and 21. The agent table holds only agents 21, 22, 23 and 25. An inner join on agent_id returns how many rows?

questions.topic: What an earlier filter removed
questions.learningObjective: compute the contribution a filter removed before the aggregate ran

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why duplication outranks loss in a bad join
questions.learningObjective: explain why a join that multiplies rows is the harder failure to notice
questions.stem: Explain why a join that silently duplicates rows is harder to catch than one that silently drops them, and say which single check catches both.

answer.exemplar: A dropped row is a subtraction and a duplicated row is a multiplication, and only one of those announces itself in a total. When a join drops the three orders whose customers are missing, the report says three orders, and anyone who knows the ledger holds six has a number to disbelieve, so the error is caught by a reader who happens to remember the source count. When a join returns 8 rows for 5 orders, the report says 8, no prior figure exists to contradict it, every value in it is a real amount, and a sample of the rows looks entirely legitimate, so the error survives every check a reader makes and is discovered, if at all, when a reconciliation months later disagrees with the books for reasons nobody can reconstruct. The one check that catches both is a row-count assertion placed on the join itself: compare the row count the join returned against the row count of the table that was supposed to come through unchanged, and fail the run when they differ. That single comparison catches the multiplication because the count grew, and it catches the loss because the count shrank, and it costs one number rather than a review of every figure in the report.

questions.explanation: The asymmetry is a fact about how errors are detected rather than about how bad they are. A dropped row leaves a total smaller than something a reader may already know, so the error has a witness; a duplicated row produces a total that is larger than the truth and matches nothing anybody remembers, so it has to be found by looking. The count assertion works for both because it is a comparison against the count the join was supposed to preserve, and a count that grew and a count that shrank are both failures of the same promise. Its cost is one number per join, which is why it belongs on every join rather than only on the ones that have been suspected.
questions.hint: Compare what each failure does to a total, and ask which one a reader has an independent figure to check against.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a key guarantees and what it cannot
questions.learningObjective: explain the boundary between what a key promises and what it cannot know
questions.stem: Explain why a primary key declared on a column is a promise about identity rather than about correctness, and give a case where the promise holds and the data is still wrong.

answer.exemplar: A primary key states that no two rows claim the same identity and that every row states one, and both statements are about the relationship between rows rather than about what any row means. The database can check them completely, because the check needs nothing but the column itself, which is exactly why a key can be enforced and a meaning cannot. So a customer table whose key is customer_id can hold a customer called with an empty name, an address that belongs to somebody else, and a row inserted by a test script last Tuesday, and every one of those rows satisfies the promise perfectly. The case that makes this concrete is an id assigned by a sequence that was reseeded during a restore, so two different real customers now share the value 1041 in two shards that were never joined; the key holds within each table, the uniqueness that mattered to the business does not exist, and every downstream figure keyed on that column is quietly double-counting. The check that would have caught it is not a constraint but a reconciliation against the source system's own identifier list.

questions.explanation: The boundary the key draws is between what can be checked from the column alone and what needs the rest of the world. Uniqueness and presence are decided entirely within the column, so a database can enforce them on every write and never be wrong about them. Meaning, correctness and provenance all require information the column does not contain, so no constraint can reach them and no amount of constraint will substitute for a reconciliation. That is why an enforced key and a trustworthy column are separate achievements, and why a schema full of constraints can still describe a table whose contents are wrong in a way that every downstream figure inherits.
questions.hint: Ask what a check on one column can establish, and what it would need in order to establish more.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why frame boundaries are worth writing out
questions.learningObjective: explain how an off-by-one frame survives review
questions.stem: Explain how a window frame that is one row out at every step produces a series that still looks right, and say what single comparison exposes it.

answer.exemplar: A running total whose frame excludes the current row is wrong at every point by exactly one term, and a uniform error of that kind is the hardest kind to see because it preserves the shape that made the series worth having. The line still rises, the last value is still the largest, and no value in it is impossible, so a reader checking that the total grows and ends high concludes the query works. What has actually happened is that the series reports the state of the world before each row rather than at it, which matters most exactly where running totals are used, at the final row, where the shortfall equals the entire current period and where a reconciliation against a balance will be out by that term every single month. The comparison that exposes it is between the last value of the series and the plain total of the underlying column, because on the last row of a partition the two must agree and here they differ by the final amount, 40 in a series ending at 75 instead of 80. Computing that one comparison for every windowed series a report depends on turns an invisible off-by-one into a failing test, and it costs one sum rather than a review of the whole series.

questions.explanation: A constant error preserves the properties a reader checks, and that is what makes it survive. Rising, ending at a maximum, staying within a plausible range: all three still hold, so a series can be wrong at every point and pass a review conducted by looking at it. The final row is where the error is largest in absolute terms and is also the row with an independent check available, because on the last row of a partition a running total must equal the plain total of the column. Comparing those two numbers is a single query, and turning it into an assertion means the off-by-one can never reach a report again.
questions.hint: Ask what the series looks like when the error is the same size at every step, and what the final row must equal.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why an offset is not a stable page
questions.learningObjective: explain why offset paging fails only when the table moves
questions.stem: Explain why paging by offset works on a table nobody is writing to and fails on a busy one, and say what a cursor names instead.

answer.exemplar: An offset says skip this many rows, which is a claim about a position in an ordering, and a position is only meaningful while nothing is inserted above it. On a table that is not being written to, paging by offset is exactly as good as paging by a cursor and considerably easier to implement, which is why it survives so long in code that works perfectly in development and perfectly in production until the first write arrives. The moment eight newer rows land, every position below them shifts down by eight, and the reader's next request silently re-reads eight rows it has already shown and skips eight it has not, so the same session sees duplicates and omissions in equal measure. The failure is intermittent and load-dependent, which is the worst property a paging bug can have: it appears under exactly the conditions where the data is most interesting, when a busy table is being read, and it disappears when anyone reproduces it on a copy. A cursor avoids the whole class by naming the last row rather than a count, so a row inserted above is never returned to that session, a row inserted below is returned once, and the reader's position is a fact about the data rather than about the table's history.

questions.explanation: The failure of offset paging is invisible in exactly the situation it is tested, which is why it survives. On a copy nobody writes to, the positions are stable, the pages tile perfectly, and the implementation looks correct, so the bug is only reachable under the one condition nobody reproduces on demand: a table being written to while it is read. The mechanism behind that is simply that an offset is a claim about a place, and a place is not a fact about a row. A cursor replaces the place with the row itself, carrying forward the last value the reader saw, and a reader that resumes from a row rather than from a count cannot be moved by anything written above it, whatever else happens to the table while it reads. The cost of the cursor is that it needs a stable ordering to resume from, which is a real requirement, and the reason the offset is often kept is that it needs no ordering discipline at all.
questions.hint: Ask whether the mechanism names a row or names a count of rows before it, and when it is tested.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a plan is read before a query is called fast
questions.learningObjective: explain what a query plan settles that a stopwatch cannot
questions.stem: Explain why a query's plan is worth reading before anyone declares it fast, and say what the plan reports that a stopwatch does not.

answer.exemplar: A stopwatch tells you how long the query took on one run in one set of circumstances, and from that number nothing follows about whether the work it did was necessary. A plan reports the quantity that explains the time, which is the number of rows examined, and a plan can therefore show you a query that takes 200 milliseconds because it read 900 rows and a query that takes four seconds because it read 900,000 to return the same 12. That comparison is the whole argument for reading plans: the two queries are indistinguishable by output and by headline timing on a small sample, and only one of them is going to survive a table that grows. The other reason to read the plan first is that it is the only artefact that names the cause, since a slow time says that something is expensive while the plan says whether that something was a scan, a nested loop over a large outer side, or a filter wrapped around an indexed column. Without the cause, the response is guesswork, and guesswork in this area reliably produces an index nobody uses and a rewrite that fixes a query nobody runs.

questions.explanation: A duration is a single number about one execution and it has no internal structure, so nothing in it can be acted on: a query that reads 900 rows and one that reads 900,000 to return the same 12 rows can differ by a thousandfold in cost while looking identical from the outside. The plan supplies the missing structure by reporting rows examined per stage, which both explains the duration and says whether the work was necessary, and that second question is the one that matters when a table is about to grow. Reading plans early is also what keeps optimisation honest, because a rewrite that lowers a duration without lowering rows examined has usually moved the cost somewhere less visible rather than removed it.
questions.hint: Ask what quantity explains a duration, and whether a duration tells you whether that quantity was necessary.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why naming a step is a debugging tool
questions.learningObjective: explain what a named intermediate result makes possible when a figure is wrong
questions.stem: Explain how naming the steps of a long join makes a wrong figure locatable, and say what it does not do for the query.

answer.exemplar: A long join computes every output column from every table at once, so a figure that is wrong cannot be attributed to any particular join, and the debugging process becomes a sequence of rewrites in which each attempt tests a different suspicion. A named step changes that by giving each intermediate result a name that can be counted, sampled and compared, so a total that should have been 660 becomes a question about a result called west_orders, and the wrong figure is localised to the step that produced it rather than to the whole expression. The step that has too many rows is obvious once it has a name and a count, and the step that lost its rows is just as obvious, so the debugging stops being a search and becomes a comparison. What naming does not do is make anything faster, guarantee that the logic is right, or make the query safe to change, and it is worth being blunt about that because the rewrite is often sold as a performance improvement, which it is not: the answer is identical before and after, and only the reader's ability to check it has changed. Where it pays is at the moment somebody else inherits the query, which is to say at the moment the numbers start being trusted.

questions.explanation: Debugging is a search, and a search is only as good as the space it searches, so the useful question about a long expression is not how to inspect it but how much there is to inspect. A named step reduces the space to a handful of countable results, each of which can be compared with what it should contain, and the comparison localises a fault in one pass instead of by elimination. The limit is worth stating plainly: naming changes nothing about what the query computes and nothing about how fast it runs, so the rewrite earns its place at the moment somebody has to change or defend the query rather than at the moment it is first written.
questions.hint: Ask what a wrong number in an unnamed expression can be attributed to, and what a name changes about that.

questions.explanation: The order follows the dependencies exactly. The grain comes first, because a report that has quietly become one row per region cannot then be fixed by choosing a better window, and the group-by that would have collapsed the orders is the failure this decision exists to prevent. Partition and ordering come next because a rank and a running total are both defined relative to them, so choosing the frame before the ordering means choosing a boundary relative to a set that does not exist yet. The frame and the ranking function belong together because they are the two places where a tie or an off-by-one can enter, and the final check on the boundary rows is the only stage that can confirm both, since the first row of a partition and the last row of one expose an incorrect frame immediately and a tie shows itself at the cutoff rather than in the middle of the list.
questions.hint: Ask which decision each later one is defined relative to, and where a mistake in each would first be visible.
